claim: Second-syllable vowel quantity in disyllabic stems is morphophonologically conditioned by suffix class and the stem-final segment: ordinary suffixes lengthen V2 unless the stem ends in no C3 or in /n, nh/; designated lengthening suffixes also lengthen after vowel-final stems but still not after nasal-final stems; shortening suffixes shorten an underlyingly long V2.

source_forms.ordinary_suffix: V2 long unless C3 is null or n/nh
source_forms.lengthening_suffix: V2 long even when C3 null, but not when C3=n/nh
source_forms.notation: lengthening suffix marked : ; shortening suffix marked $

normalized_environment: V2 quantity conditioned jointly by disyllabic stem domain, C3 class, and suffix class
scope: inflectional and derivational suffixation of disyllabic stems
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The source states that the three behavioral classes characterize all inflectional and derivational suffixes, but the quantity process itself is restricted by stem shape and final-segment class.
table_figure: prose with ordinary, lengthening and shortening suffix classes

claim: Suffix-triggered lengthening and shortening target the second syllable of disyllabic stems; vowel length in monosyllabic stems and trisyllabic-or-longer stems is unaffected by these suffixes.
normalized_environment: quantity alternation domain = σ2 of disyllabic stem only
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The explicit non-target domains are part of the generalization and prevent treating suffixal quantity as an unrestricted preceding-vowel process.

claim: Main stress is quantity-sensitive within the initial two-syllable window: if the first two vowels are short, stress is initial; a long first vowel also bears initial main stress; but a short first vowel followed by a long second vowel shifts main stress to the second syllable. Closed syllables do not independently attract stress.

source_forms.coda_weight: closed syllables do not attract main stress

normalized_environment: main stress defaults σ1; Vː in σ2 attracts stress iff σ1 short; coda C is not stress-weight-bearing
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Words with long vowels in both σ1 and σ2 are analytically disputed and are staged separately rather than forced into this rule.

claim: Secondary stress follows a left-to-right disyllabic rhythm but shifts to avoid clashes: with initial main stress it normally falls on subsequent odd-numbered syllables; when main stress is on σ2, the secondary-stress series is correspondingly pushed right onto even-numbered syllables.

source_forms.default: trochaic/disyllabic rhythm; secondary stress on later odd syllables after σ1 main stress
source_forms.σ2_main: secondary stresses on later even syllables

normalized_environment: secondary stress every two syllables from main-stress anchor; shift right to avoid adjacent stresses
exceptions_or_counterexamples: A final odd syllable receives secondary stress only when this does not create a clash; the rhythm is therefore prosodically conditioned rather than a simple parity rule.
section: 3.2 Distribution of secondary stresses and clash avoidance

claim: A final odd-numbered syllable can bear secondary stress even when open, provided this does not create a stress clash; the same position remains unstressed when secondary stress there would be adjacent to another stress.

source_forms.licensed: final odd σ gets secondary stress if no clash, including open σ
source_forms.blocked: final odd σ unstressed if secondary stress would create clash

normalized_environment: final secondary stress licensed by rhythm, blocked by clash; openness does not block it
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The explicit clash condition overrides the otherwise expected rhythmic stress.
section: 3.2 Distribution of secondary stresses and clash avoidance

claim: The status of words with long vowels in both initial syllables is analytically disputed: Haviland transcribed both syllables as main-stressed, whereas Elías-Ulloa argues from secondary-stress and clash behavior that only σ1 is a metrical head and σ2 is unstressed.

source_forms.Haviland_1979: two initial long-vowel syllables described/transcribed as equally main-stressed
source_forms.Elias_Ulloa_2020: only initial syllable is main-stressed; second long-vowel syllable lacks head behavior

normalized_environment: HH-initial stress status unresolved across analyses; preserve competing descriptions
scope: words with long vowels in both first and second syllables
exceptions_or_counterexamples: This record intentionally does not collapse the disagreement into a categorical language fact; the later analysis is an argument based on phonological behavior, while the primary descriptive transcription differs.
